questions.q: How does a review board differ from the solo checklist review taught in Lesson 21?
options: A review board eliminates the need for any checklist items
A review board only evaluates cost, never technical trade-offs

A review board is a structured, multi-person process where a panel questions the design's author directly and in real time, which can surface reasoning gaps that a written document might hide behind confident prose
A review board and a solo checklist are functionally identical in every respect
questions.explain: The shift from a solo written checklist to a live panel matters because direct, real-time questioning forces the author to actually articulate their reasoning, exposing gaps that a well-written document could otherwise paper over.

questions.q: What are reviewers in Salesforce's CTA review board actually evaluating, per this lesson?
options: Whether the candidate can justify their specific choices with sound reasoning, identify the trade-offs their design accepts, and respond credibly to pushback — multiple reasonable designs can pass
Whether the candidate proposed the one single "correct" architecture
Whether the candidate memorized the most governor limit numbers
Whether the candidate's design matches a fixed answer key exactly
questions.explain: The CTA board doesn't require one specific 'correct' design — multiple reasonable architectures can pass — what's evaluated is the quality of the candidate's reasoning, trade-off awareness, and ability to defend choices credibly under questioning.

questions.q: What four elements does this lesson say make up a strong defense of a design decision under review-board questioning?
options: The decision's cost, its vendor, its release date, and its documentation link
A list of every Salesforce feature used in the design, regardless of relevance
Only restating the decision with more confidence when pushed
The decision itself, the specific facts that drove it, the trade-off being accepted and why it's acceptable, and at least one alternative considered and why it was rejected
questions.explain: A strong defense names the decision, ties it to specific scenario facts, explicitly states the accepted trade-off and its justification, and names a rejected alternative with reasoning — the structure modeled in this lesson's practice script.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as a sign of a weak defense under review-board questioning?
options: Calmly explaining the specific trade-off being accepted
Restating the original decision without its underlying reasoning, or abandoning a genuinely sound decision the moment a reviewer pushes back
Naming a rejected alternative and explaining why it was rejected
Citing the specific scenario facts that drove the decision
questions.explain: A weak defense either repeats the decision louder without reasoning behind it, or caves on a well-reasoned choice the moment a reviewer pushes — both signal that the original decision wasn't actually thought through, just assumed.

questions.q: In the practice script defending the asynchronous order-to-WMS flow, why does the defense specifically cite the idempotency key when responding to the suggestion of making the flow synchronous instead?
options: Because idempotency keys have nothing to do with the defense and were mentioned only in passing
Because idempotency keys are required by Salesforce's terms of service for any asynchronous integration

Because it shows the asynchronous design doesn't trade away safety to get decoupling — a retry after an ambiguous failure can't cause a duplicate fulfillment, addressing the reviewer's underlying safety concern without needing to go synchronous
Because the idempotency key makes the WMS callout synchronous after all
questions.explain: Citing the idempotency key directly answers the implicit safety concern behind the reviewer's question — showing that the asynchronous design achieves safety (no duplicate fulfillment on retry) without needing the availability-coupling cost of going synchronous.
